title: Hosted API soft-commit protocol and SDK ergonomics
body:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a 'soft-commit' protocol for the Hosted API that makes tool-calls and structured partial output interruptible, resumable, and safe for low-bandwidth/mobile clients and high-concurrency servers. The goal is to let SDKs and clients receive usable partial results quickly, allow the server to gracefully retract/replace parts when better data arrives, and provide clear semantics for idempotency and billing while preserving safety and observability.

Motivation / problems we see:
- Mobile/edge clients often need an early partial answer to render UI while a long-running toolchain executes (eg: fetch + rerank + external tool). Current streaming semantics are either raw token streams or final JSON blobs; neither expresses a partially-validated structured sub-result that can be shown and updated.
- Long tool fanout (calling multiple external services) produces multiple partial items that may arrive out of order. Clients need a consistent way to bind, replace, or cancel these fragments.
- Existing SDK patterns push complexity into clients (manual dedupe, patch merging, ad-hoc timeouts). We want an SDK-first protocol with ergonomic primitives (soft-commit, optimistic preview, consistent conflict resolution).

Key concepts (high level):
- Fragment: a named structured partial result (small JSON) with an id and a schema type (eg: summary.v1, action-candidate.v2, citation-block.v1).
- Soft-commit: server marks a fragment as 'soft-committed' meaning it is usable but may be updated or revoked. Soft-commit carries a version token and a TTL.
- Hard-commit: server marks a fragment as finalized; replaces are only allowed via a new hard-commit with higher sequence. Hard-commit triggers billing checkpoint semantics (configurable).
- Synthetic-ACK: client-facing lightweight acknowledgement shape delivered by server that indicates fragment receipt and provisional validation state; not an RPC level ACK but a semantic one for the application layer.
- Reconciliation hints: small metadata attached to fragments to help SDKs merge (merge_mode: replace/append/patch; conflict_strategy: newest-wins/score-based/merge-preserve).

Protocol wire (example event stream entries):
- EVENT: fragment.create {fragment_id, schema, proto_payload, soft_commit_version, ttl_seconds, hints}
- EVENT: fragment.update {fragment_id, soft_commit_version, proto_payload_delta, hints}
- EVENT: fragment.revoke {fragment_id, reason, revocation_version}
- EVENT: fragment.finalize {fragment_id, hard_commit_seq, final_payload}
- EVENT: heartbeat /keepalive

Payload constraints:
- Fragments are small (recommended < 16KB). Larger results should be chunked into multiple fragments with sequencing metadata.
- Server must include schema_version string so SDKs can pick validators/parsers.
- Delta updates should be expressed as JSON Patch (RFC 6902) or simple replace, indicated by hints.merge_mode.

SDK ergonomics: what the client libraries provide out of box:
1) Fragment store: local in-memory map keyed by fragment_id, exposes getLive(fragment_id) returning the latest soft or hard state and helper events (onProvisional, onFinal, onRevoked).
2) Optimistic preview helpers: UI-friendly primitives that render soft-commits with translucency/'stale' markers, automatically switch to final when hard-commit received.
3) Merge strategies: default newest-wins but pluggable user-provided mergeFn(fragmentA, fragmentB) for complex apps.
4) Backpressure and prefetch policy: SDK exposes a config to limit concurrent live fragments and to defer non-critical fragments until network stable (useful for mobile).
5) Idempotency tokens: SDK binds outgoing requests to client-generated idempotency keys so reconnects or retries can be deduped server-side.
6) Reconnect & resume: SDK accepts last-seen soft_commit_version per fragment to request missed updates after reconnect. Automatic rehydration APIs for reloading UI state from a snapshot endpoint.

Billing / visibility model (ops product considerations):
- Soft-commit events do not necessarily advance billing unless they include a heavy compute marker. Product can expose a per-fragment cost_estimate to help clients budget.
- Hard-commit should be the canonical meter checkpoint for most usage-based pricing. We will support a config flag on model/route to allow soft-commit checkpointing for long-running tasks requiring incremental billing.
- Console will show fragment timelines per request: creation, updates, revocations, finalization, and tool-call latencies.

Safety & retries (security / correctness):
- Revocation must be auditable: fragment.revoke events recorded with reason and optional signature for private deployments.
- Tool calls that produce fragments must include provenance fields (tool_id, tool_request_id) to correlate retries & failures.
- SDK enforces a conservative default to not auto-apply revoked fragments to persisted app state unless the app opts in.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Server can emit event stream with fragment.create/update/finalize/events for the hosted-api streaming route.
- JS and Python SDKs provide a FragmentStore with onProvisional/onFinal hooks and a simple optimistic preview renderer example.
- Console shows fragment timeline for at least the last 30 days for sampled traffic and per-request fragment counts.
- Test harness includes network drop/reconnect scenarios and verifies idempotency semantics.

Open questions (to resolve in follow-ups):
- Default billing semantics for soft-commit: free vs metered vs configurable checkpoint.
- TTL policy: automatic revocation after TTL or passive expiry (server-side GC vs client-side stale tagging).
- Schema negotiation strategy across SDK versions. Do we rely on schema strings + server-side adaptor mapping or enforce semantic schema registry?

Rollout plan / milestones:
- Phase 0 (experiment): a feature-flagged server stream + JS SDK dev-preview (6 weeks). Keep it opt-in per route.
- Phase 1 (beta): expand to Python SDK, Console fragment timelines, add telemetry (fragment lifetimes, update counts, revocations) (12 weeks).
- Phase 2 (GA): hard-commit billing path, mobile SDK integrations (iOS/Android), docs + migration guide (16 weeks).

Telemetry & success metrics:
- median time to first soft-commit (target < 400ms for common prompt profiles).
- fraction of requests that deliver at least one soft-commit before finalization (target 75% for prioritized routes).
- update churn per fragment (want low churn; flag high-churn workloads for optimization).
- client reconnection success rate and resume delta loss rate.

Developer experience notes / examples:
- Simple use-case: search assistant issues 3 external tool calls (scrape, fetch-authoritative, reranker). Server emits three fragments: candidate-list.soft (soft-commit), rerank.soft (soft-commit), final-summary.final (hard-commit). SDK shows candidate-list immediately; when rerank.final arrives it replaces candidate list with scores.
- Error handling: if a tool fails, server emits fragment.revoke with reason and optional fallback fragment (eg: degraded-summary.soft). SDK exposes onRevoked so app can surface fallback copy.

Security / compliance implications:
- Fragment provenance must be stored in audit logs for Private deployments.
- For regulated customers, we will offer an option to disable soft-commit (force final-only) to avoid surface of provisional data.

Implementation risks and mitigation:
- Risk: high update churn causes excessive client CPU/network. Mitigation: enforce fragment size and update rate limits server-side; provide sampling for high-frequency updates.
- Risk: client libraries diverge in merge semantics. Mitigation: ship canonical merge strategies and unit tests across SDKs; provide conformance tests.

Next actions (owners):
- Engineering (serving-runtime): prototype server-side fragment event format + sample route (owner: Marcus Patel).
- SDK (devx): implement FragmentStore in JS and Python, example React component for optimistic preview (owner: Sofia Alvarez).
- Product/Console: wire fragment timeline to request detail panel, gated by feature flag (owner: Diego Martins).
- Security: review revocation audit design for Private customers (owner: Priya Rao).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally prescriptive on SDK ergonomics; design tradeoffs are to reduce app-level complexity. Please call out any platform-level constraints (esp. on billing and storage costs) early.
summary: Proposal for a soft-commit protocol that exposes named structured partial results (fragments) via streaming events with versioning, TTLs, and reconciliation hints plus SDK features (FragmentStore, optimistic preview, merge strategies). Includes MVP acceptance criteria, rollout plan, telemetry targets, and open questions.
